analogy.p: Imagine a row of seats in a cinema that is completely full: nobody can join the row, and nobody needs to leave. The noble gas atom's full outer shell is like this row, so it does not take, give away or share electrons with any other atom. Other elements are like people with empty or one spare seat who go looking for a way to complete their row. The analogy breaks down because electrons can actually be removed from a noble gas with enough energy, whereas people in a cinema are free to leave at any time; 'unreactive' means very hard, not impossible.

bullets: Group 0 elements: **helium (He), neon (Ne), argon (Ar), krypton (Kr), xenon (Xe) and radon (Rn)**. At GCSE you mainly need He, Ne and Ar for electron arrangements.
Group 0 is on the **far right** of the periodic table, after the halogens (Group 7).
The elements in a group have **similar chemical properties because they have the same number of electrons in their outer shell** (this is the key periodic-table idea).
'Noble' comes from the idea that these gases were too 'aloof' to react, like nobility who do not mix; they are also called the **inert gases** (inert = unreactive).
Radon is **radioactive**, so it is not used much, but it still fits the same pattern of properties.

Link to other topics: the periodic table is arranged by **atomic number** in **periods** (rows) and **groups** (columns); the group number tells you the number of outer-shell electrons (except helium and Group 0 which is 'full').
core.h: 1. Where Group 0 sits and what the name means
core.p: The **noble gases** make up **Group 0** (the far right-hand column) of the periodic table: **helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon**. The group is called Group 0 because its elements have essentially **zero tendency to react**: their atoms do not need to gain, lose or share electrons. Every element in the group is a gas at room temperature, and the group is the clearest example of how an element's chemistry is controlled by its **electron arrangement** (the number of electrons in its outer shell).

bullets: **Helium: 2** (one full shell, so only 2 outer electrons). It is a common mistake to say helium has 8.
**Neon: 2,8** (full second shell, 8 outer electrons).
**Argon: 2,8,8** (full third shell for the first 20 elements, 8 outer electrons).
Krypton, xenon and radon each have **8 electrons in the outer shell** (they have more inner shells, which you do not need to draw).

Other elements react in order to reach a full outer shell by **losing electrons** (metals, forming positive ions), **gaining electrons** (non-metals, forming negative ions), or **sharing electrons** (covalent bonds). Noble gases are already there, so they do not need to.
Spec link: the chemical properties of elements are related to the **arrangement of electrons in their atoms and the number of electrons in the outer shell**.
core.h: 2. Electron arrangements: the reason for everything
core.p: Electrons occupy **shells (energy levels)** around the nucleus. The first shell holds a maximum of **2** electrons, and the second and third shells hold up to **8** (at GCSE, for the first 20 elements). The noble gases have a **completely full outer shell**. This is called a **stable arrangement of electrons**, and it is the single most important idea in the topic. Because the outer shell is already full, noble gas atoms have no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons.

bullets: Model sentence for 2 marks: 'They have a **full outer shell of electrons**, so they do not need to **gain, lose or share electrons**.'
They do not form ionic bonds because they do not lose or gain electrons easily, and they do not form covalent bonds because they do not need to share electrons.
Do not say 'because they are gases' or 'because they have eight electrons' (helium has two); the reason is the **full outer shell / stable electron arrangement**.
'Unreactive' means very low chemical reactivity under normal conditions; the extremely rare compounds of xenon and krypton are beyond GCSE.
Because they do not form compounds, in the air they are found as **separate atoms**, not as molecules like O₂ or N₂.
Link to bonding: ionic compounds form between metals and non-metals (electron transfer), covalent compounds between non-metals (sharing); noble gases do neither.
core.h: 3. Why noble gases are unreactive (model explanation)
core.p: Noble gases are **unreactive** and **do not easily form molecules** because their atoms have **stable arrangements of electrons** (full outer shells). Reactions happen when atoms gain, lose or share electrons to reach a full outer shell. Since noble gas atoms already have one, there is nothing to be gained by reacting, and a lot of energy would be needed to remove electrons from or force extra electrons into a full shell. So no **ionic bonds** (transfer of electrons) or **covalent bonds** (sharing of electrons) form.

bullets: Chemical formulae of the noble gases are simply **He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn** with no subscripts.
In a diagram of a noble gas, show **separate circles (atoms) spaced far apart**, not pairs joined together.
Particles in a gas are far apart and move randomly and quickly; in a noble gas the forces between them are very weak, which is why they are gases at room temperature.
Do not write 'He₂' or 'Ar₂'; this would be an error.
Monatomic gases do not conduct electricity as a gas because they contain no mobile charged particles (no free ions or delocalised electrons).
Link: in a molecule the covalent bond is **strong**; between neighbouring noble gas atoms there is only a **weak intermolecular-type force**.
core.p: Because noble gas atoms do not bond to one another, the gases are made of **single, separate atoms**. This is described as **monatomic** (mono = one). Compare this with oxygen (O₂), nitrogen (N₂) and chlorine (Cl₂), which are **diatomic** molecules, two atoms joined by a covalent bond. In a sample of neon gas, the particles are individual Ne atoms moving randomly, with only very **weak forces of attraction between atoms**.

bullets: Colourless, odourless gases at room temperature (they do glow in coloured light when electricity passes through them in a discharge tube, but this is not a colour of the gas itself).
**Very low boiling points**, all below 0 °C (helium boils at about −269 °C, close to absolute zero).
**Non-flammable**: they will not burn or support burning.
**Density increases down the group** because the atoms get heavier (see section 7); helium is much less dense than air, argon is denser than air.
They do not conduct electricity in the gas state (no free charged particles).
Link: they are all gases because at 20 °C the temperature is well above their boiling points (the highest, radon, is about −62 °C).
core.h: 5. Physical properties of the noble gases
core.p: All the noble gases are **colourless gases at room temperature** with very **low melting and boiling points**. They are **non-flammable** (they do not burn), because burning is a reaction with oxygen and they do not react. They are poor conductors of heat and electricity. These properties follow from the monatomic structure: weak forces between separate atoms need very little energy to overcome, so they boil at extremely low temperatures.

bullets: State the trend precisely: '**boiling point increases down the group**' (or 'as relative atomic mass increases').
Because every value is below 0 °C, all the noble gases are **gases** at room temperature (about 20 °C).
The numbers are **negative**: −269 is a much lower temperature than −62. Common error: saying helium has the highest boiling point.
To **predict**, estimate between neighbouring values: krypton lies between argon (−186 °C) and xenon (−108 °C), so a sensible estimate is about −150 °C.
The graph is a smooth curve rising, not a straight line, so a linear estimate is only approximate; use 'approximately' when quoting.
Link to states of matter: a substance boils when particles have enough energy to overcome the forces between them; the stronger the forces, the higher the boiling point.
core.h: 6. Boiling point trend: increases down the group
core.p: The boiling points of the noble gases **increase with increasing relative atomic mass (going down the group)**. Approximate values are: **helium −269 °C, neon −246 °C, argon −186 °C, krypton −153 °C, xenon −108 °C, radon −62 °C**. This pattern must be stated as a trend in your answers, and you should be able to use it to predict the boiling point of an element in the group from its neighbours.

bullets: Key phrase: 'as the atoms get bigger/ have more electrons, the **forces between the atoms are stronger**'.
'More **energy** is needed to **overcome the forces** between the atoms' – note you overcome forces, you do **not** break covalent bonds.
Never write 'the bonds between atoms get stronger': there are **no bonds** between the atoms of a noble gas.
Same logic is used in 4.2 for simple covalent molecules: larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces and higher boiling points.

Density: at the same temperature and pressure, equal volumes of gas contain the same number of atoms, so a gas with heavier atoms has a greater mass per volume (greater density). Argon (relative atomic mass 40) is denser than air (average about 29); helium (4) is much less dense.
Link: the same trend (boiling point rises with atomic or molecular size) is seen for the halogens in Group 7, though those are diatomic molecules.
core.h: 7. Explaining the trend: forces between atoms (Higher-quality answer)
core.p: Going down Group 0, the **atoms get larger and have more electrons** (more shells), and the relative atomic mass increases. This makes the **intermolecular forces (the attractions between the atoms) stronger**. Boiling involves overcoming only these weak forces (not breaking any bonds), so the **stronger the forces, the more energy is needed to separate the atoms and the higher the boiling point**. A full-mark answer always links: size/mass → stronger forces → more energy → higher boiling point.

bullets: **Helium** in balloons and airships: **less dense than air** and **non-flammable** (hydrogen is also light but explosive, so helium is safer).
**Argon** in filament light bulbs and as a shielding gas in welding: it is **unreactive**, so it stops the hot filament or metal reacting with oxygen in the air.
**Neon** in advertising signs: glows with a coloured light when electricity passes through it.
**Argon/other noble gases** can be used to fill containers to provide an **inert atmosphere** where air would cause oxidation.
Always state the property and the use: 'it is **unreactive** so it prevents the filament from burning away'.
These uses are applications of the properties; the specification tests the properties and trends, so exam questions on uses will provide context and expect you to apply 'unreactive' or 'low density'.
core.h: 8. Uses of the noble gases (apply the properties)
core.p: The uses of the noble gases follow directly from two properties: they are **unreactive (inert)**, and some have **very low density** or give coloured light in a discharge tube. Exam questions give you an unfamiliar use and ask you to explain it, so you must link the use to a property.

bullets: Group 1: 1 outer electron, **lose** it, form **1+** ions; reactivity **increases** down the group.
Group 7: 7 outer electrons, **gain** 1 electron, form **1−** ions or share (covalent); reactivity **decreases** down the group.
Group 0: **full** outer shell, do **not** react.
Boiling points: Group 0 and Group 7 both **increase** down the group; Group 1 melting and boiling points **decrease** down the group.
Group number = number of outer electrons for Groups 1 to 7; Group 0 has full outer shells (8, or 2 for helium).
Link: this comparison is often a 4 to 6 mark question; link each group to its electron arrangement.
core.h: 9. Group 0 compared with Group 1 and Group 7
core.p: Comparing groups shows how electron arrangement controls reactivity. **Group 1 (alkali metals)** have one outer electron, which is easily lost, so they are very reactive. **Group 7 (halogens)** have seven outer electrons and easily gain one, so they are reactive non-metals. **Group 0** has a full outer shell so they are unreactive. Reactivity within Groups 1 and 7 changes down the group, but Group 0 stays unreactive throughout.

bullets: **Describe**: 'boiling point increases as relative atomic mass increases / down the group', then quote two values with units (°C).
**Predict** (interpolation): value of an unlisted gas lies between its neighbours; the estimate should sit between them.
**Extrapolate** (e.g. a possible element below radon): the boiling point would be **higher** than radon's −62 °C, but it is less reliable because it is beyond the data.
**State at room temperature**: compare room temperature (20 °C) with the boiling point: if 20 °C is above the boiling point, it is a gas.
**Axes**: boiling point on the y-axis in °C, with negative numbers; take care reading negative scales.
**Calculate a change**: from argon to krypton the boiling point rises by −153 − (−186) = 33 °C; take care when subtracting negative numbers.
core.h: 10. Reading and using data about the noble gases
core.p: You may be given a table or graph of boiling points, melting points or density and asked to describe a pattern, predict a missing value, or explain it. Treat this as a standard skill: describe the trend using the numbers, quote units, and use the stated trend to predict.

bullets: Simple molecular substances have **low melting and boiling points** because the intermolecular forces are weak; this applies equally to monatomic noble gases.
They do not conduct electricity because they have **no mobile charged particles** (no free electrons or ions).
Contrast with **ionic compounds** (strong electrostatic forces, high melting points) and **metals** (delocalised electrons).
Noble gases are the only elements that exist as **single atoms** at room temperature and pressure.
When asked 'what are the forces being overcome when argon boils?', the answer is **weak forces between atoms (intermolecular forces)**, not covalent bonds.
Link: at A level and beyond you will name these as London (dispersion) forces; at GCSE just say intermolecular forces.
core.h: 11. How this links to bonding and structure (4.2)
core.p: The behaviour of noble gases is a first example of the structure and bonding ideas you meet in more detail later. Noble gas atoms are held together only by weak **intermolecular forces** in the liquid and solid states, in the same way as small simple molecular substances, which explains their very low melting and boiling points. They have no bonds, no ions and no free electrons, so they never conduct electricity.

bullets: Air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, about 0.9% argon, 0.04% carbon dioxide, plus small amounts of other noble gases and water vapour.
Their chemical inertness explains why the noble gases were not discovered earlier: they did not form compounds that could be detected.
Mendeleev arranged elements by atomic mass and properties, and left gaps for undiscovered elements; the later discovery of the noble gases added a new group to the table.
Spec link: you should know that the modern periodic table orders elements by **atomic number** and that elements with the same number of outer electrons share a group.
Link: 'noble gases do not react' is why they are safe to use where a flammable or reactive gas would be dangerous.
Radon is a radioactive gas produced by the decay of uranium in rocks; it is a health hazard in some buildings, a link to the radioactivity topic in physics.
core.h: 12. Link to the atmosphere and the Periodic Table's history
core.p: Argon makes up roughly 1% (about 0.9%) of dry air, which is why it is the cheapest and most commonly used noble gas. Since the noble gases do not react, their percentages in the atmosphere have stayed fixed over time. In the development of the periodic table, the noble gases were discovered late, in the 1890s, and slotted into a new group on the right-hand side without disturbing the order, which supported the table's pattern.

exam: 1 mark: state a fact, e.g. 'Group 0 elements are unreactive' or 'Boiling point increases down the group'. Write it as a clear single statement.
2 marks 'Explain why noble gases are unreactive': (1) full outer shell / stable electron arrangement; (2) so they do not need to gain, lose or share electrons.
'Describe the trend' (2 marks): state the direction ('boiling point increases down the group'), then support with two data values and units, e.g. from −269 °C to −62 °C.
'Predict' command word: give a value or state between the neighbouring values and say it is based on the trend; use the correct sign and unit.

'Explain the trend in boiling point' (3 to 4 marks): bigger atoms / more electrons → stronger intermolecular forces (between atoms) → more energy needed to overcome them → higher boiling point. Never mention breaking covalent bonds.
Draw electron arrangement diagrams carefully: He has 2 on one shell; Ne 2,8; Ar 2,8,8. Fill inner shells first and use crosses or dots.
6-mark comparison questions: link each group (1, 7, 0) to its number of outer electrons, then to reactivity and the trend down the group.
Use of noble gases: always state the property then the use (unreactive → inert atmosphere; low density and non-flammable → balloons).
In graph or table questions, check the sign of the numbers: −269 is lower than −186.
Use the phrase 'monatomic' with its meaning ('single atoms') if asked why the gases do not form molecules or why they are gases.

mistakes.r: They have a **full outer shell**; helium has only 2 electrons, which fills the first shell.
mistakes.w: Noble gases are unreactive because they have 8 electrons in the outer shell (for all of them).

mistakes.r: There are **no bonds** between noble gas atoms; the **intermolecular forces** (attractions between atoms) get stronger as the atoms get bigger.
mistakes.w: Boiling point increases because the bonds between the atoms get stronger.

mistakes.r: They are **monatomic**: single atoms, written He, Ne, Ar.
mistakes.w: Noble gases are molecules such as He₂.

mistakes.r: Reactivity depends on **electron arrangement**; many gases such as oxygen and chlorine are very reactive.
mistakes.w: They are unreactive because they are gases.

mistakes.r: −269 °C is the **lowest** boiling point; radon (−62 °C) is the highest.
mistakes.w: Helium has the highest boiling point because −269 is the biggest number.

mistakes.r: Boiling overcomes the **weak forces between atoms** only; no covalent bonds are present.
mistakes.w: Boiling noble gases breaks covalent bonds.

mistakes.r: Group 0 elements are all unreactive; it is the **boiling point** that increases down the group.
This is circular; give the reason: they have a **stable arrangement of electrons (full outer shell)**.
mistakes.w: Noble gases are unreactive because they are inert so they do not react.

mistakes.r: Noble gases are **colourless**; neon only glows red-orange in a discharge tube when electricity passes through it.
mistakes.w: They have a colour such as red for neon.

summary: You must know that the noble gases are in Group 0, are unreactive and do not easily form molecules because their atoms have stable arrangements of electrons (full outer shells), and that their boiling points increase down the group with increasing relative atomic mass. This matters because it shows how electron arrangement controls reactivity and how trends in a group let you predict properties.

terms.d: The elements in the last column of the periodic table (helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, radon); unreactive gases with full outer shells.
The highest occupied energy level of an atom; the number of electrons in it determines the chemical properties of the element.
A full outer shell of electrons, which means the atom has no tendency to gain, lose or share electrons.
Does not easily undergo chemical reactions; noble gases are unreactive because of their stable electron arrangements.
Chemically unreactive; another word for the behaviour of noble gases.
Made of single, separate atoms rather than molecules; noble gases are monatomic.
Made of molecules containing two atoms joined by a covalent bond, for example O₂, N₂, Cl₂.
The average mass of the atoms of an element compared with one twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom; it increases down Group 0.
The temperature at which a liquid becomes a gas; for the noble gases it increases down the group.
Weak attractions between neighbouring particles (molecules or, for noble gases, atoms) that are overcome when a substance melts or boils.
A region around the nucleus where electrons are found; the first shell holds up to 2 electrons and the next shells up to 8.
Electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by the transfer of electrons; noble gases do not form them.
A shared pair of electrons between non-metal atoms; noble gases do not form them.
Mass per unit volume; it increases down Group 0 because the atoms get heavier.
Does not burn; noble gases do not react with oxygen.
The number of protons in an atom, which is the order in which elements are arranged in the periodic table.

worked.ans: Argon is unreactive because it has a full outer shell of electrons (a stable arrangement), so it does not need to gain, lose or share electrons. It stops the hot filament reacting with (burning in) oxygen from the air, so the filament lasts longer.
worked.q: Explain why argon is used to fill filament lamps (3 marks).
steps: Identify the property: argon is unreactive (inert).
Explain why: it has a full outer shell of electrons (2,8,8) so does not react.
Apply: the very hot tungsten filament would burn in oxygen if air were present.

worked.q: The boiling points of argon and xenon are −186 °C and −108 °C. Estimate the boiling point of krypton and explain why your estimate is not exact (3 marks).
steps: Krypton lies between argon and xenon, so its boiling point should lie between −186 and −108.
The graph of boiling point against relative atomic mass is a curve, not a straight line, so using the mean is only an approximation.

worked.ans: Xenon atoms are bigger and have more electrons than neon atoms, so the forces between xenon atoms are stronger. More energy is needed to overcome these forces, so xenon has the higher boiling point (−108 °C compared with −246 °C). No covalent bonds are broken because the gases are monatomic.
worked.q: Explain why the boiling point of xenon is higher than the boiling point of neon (4 marks).
steps: Xenon atoms are larger / have more electrons / higher relative atomic mass.
So the intermolecular forces (between atoms) are stronger.
So more energy is needed to overcome these forces.
So the boiling point is higher.
